newsitem.title: CANADA: Alberta investors bet on Small Oil for next gusher.
newsitem.headline: Alberta investors bet on Small Oil for next gusher.

text.p: Forget high-tech stocks. You can keep your speculative gold plays. Never mind those stuffy banks. Any red-blooded Alberta investor will tell you -- good, old homegrown junior oil companies are the place to be.

Junior oils, usually start-up firms that pump out revenues of less than C$10 million ($7.3 million) with just a handful of employees, represent the freewheeling sector of Canada's energy industry, where "significant growth" is the mantra.

Most juniors are too small to be under the microscopes of major brokerages and institutional investors, so shareholders are of the retail variety looking for the next big gusher that will double, triple or quadruple a firm's stock price.
With Alberta's heritage as Canada's major oil producing region, its investors know what to look for in small oil firms, most of which trade on the Alberta Stock Exchange in Calgary.

"This is an oil and gas town and I think people look first to put their money in oil and gas," said Keith Macdonald, who heads the finance committee for the Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada (SEPAC), which represents more than 400 juniors.
"A lot of the retail investors work for oil companies and service companies, so they have some basic knowledge and want to pick the next winner."
If an investment symposium held this week for juniors was anything to go by, interest in oil's little guys remains hot, especially with today's strong oil prices and low Canadian interest rates.
The event, sponsored by SEPAC, was packed with would-be stock pickers, attired both in suits and ties as well as jeans and baseball caps.

Attracted by newspaper ads, about 800 investors crammed a sweltering hotel ballroom with seating for 650 to hear 16 juniors tell their stories. It was a loud and casual affair where attendees shouted out questions and slide presentations did not always work as planned.

But that did not matter. Investors, scared away from gold plays by recent infamous salting scandals and uninterested in blue chips whose sheer size prevent big percentage growth, were attracted to the potential gains of such firms as Founders Energy Ltd., Electra Energy Corp. and Big Horn Resources Ltd.

"If you're producing 100 barrels and you go to 200 barrels, you've doubled, right? Some of the juniors will rise more quickly than the big ones -- they're more risky but the returns can be higher," said Roland Baert, a mechanical engineer who showed up to check out the action.

For inspiration, investors look to such companies as Renaissance Energy Ltd. and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd., which grew from producing hundreds of barrels of oil a day in the 1980s to being among Canada's biggest producers and busiest drillers with market values in the billions of dollars.
"Growth in this business can be significant," said Tom Buchanan, chief executive of Founders Energy, which produces 1,500 barrels of oil a day, mostly in southeast Saskatchewan.
"You can achieve 50 or 100 percent growth over a period of three to four years quite easily if you have an aggressive exploration and exploitation programme ahead of you."
It is often the more entrepreneurial juniors that discover the big oil plays that larger companies have the cash to develop.
Without the complexities of major oil companies to worry about, Alberta investors like the chances of one or two wells doubling a firm's size in the oil province they know best.

"The drilling is in and around Alberta, Saskatchewan and northeast British Columbia," said Steve Smith, analyst with brokerage Nesbitt Burns. "A lot of these people see the drilling. Some of them even have leasehold rights on it. It's a lot more personal."
